newsitem.title: UK: UK tightens curbs on arms exports.
newsitem.headline: UK tightens curbs on arms exports.

text.p: Britain's new Labour government on Monday fulfilled its election promise to ban arms sales to countries with poor human rights records that might use them for internal repression.

Britain, one of the world's leading defence exporters, will also turn down licence applications if there is a clear risk that the arms will be used aggressively against another country, Foreign Secretary Robin Cook told parliament.

But he disappointed arms campaigners by refusing to withdraw more than 21,000 existing defence licences, including one for the controversial sale of 16 British Aerospace Hawk jets and armoured vehicles to Indonesia.

Human rights activists, who contend that the jets have been used against opponents in the breakaway East Timor region, said they would protest against the government's decision on Tuesday outside Prime Minister Tony Blair's 10 Downing Street residence.

"Whilst we welcome steps towards strengthening arms sales criteria, we are extremely disappointed that the Labour government will not revoke any existing licences," Will McMahon of the Campaign Against Arms Trade said.

"The people of East Timor and the democratic movements of Indonesia have a right to expect more firm action from a government committed to an ethical foreign policy," McMahon said in a statement after meeting Cook.
The government says it has no firm evidence that Jakarta has used Hawk jets in East Timor.
Moreover, its lawyers advised it was not realistic to revoke licences issued by the previous Conservative government, routed in the May 1 election after 18 years in power.
"It is not practical to backdate these new criteria," Cook said in a written parliamentary answer.
In a related move, Cook said Britain was also banning the export in any circumstances of electro-shock batons, stun guns, leg-irons or similar instruments of torture.
Officials said the new guidelines on arms exports hardened the Labour government's position in two respects.
Firstly, in deciding whether to licence weapons sales, officials must consider if the would-be buyer has used "similar equipment" sold by other countries for internal repression.

Secondly, the threshold for banning exports has been lowered. Whereas Labour spoke previously of weapons that were "likely" to be used for internal repression, Cook said the ban would apply if the arms "might" be used for repressive purposes.
The criteria will stop the sale of equipment with "obvious application for internal repression, in cases where the recipient country has a significant continuing record of such repression".
He said the government would pay special attention to equipment with obvious potential for use in cracking down on protesters, such as armoured personnel carriers.
Officials declined to say whether this was a reference to Indonesia, and Cook himself named no countries in his statement.
"They are universal criteria. They are not aimed at any one country in particular, but they will apply even-handedly to all countries," he said.
